sentences: Chapter 12
Stay Out of Trouble: Data, Promises, and Compliance
When you hire a person, a century of employment law tells you what you owe each other.
When you hire the machine, one Canadian tribunal held Air Canada responsible on one set of facts.
That is not a universal liability rule; it is enough reason for a conservative operating rule: be prepared to answer for what your tools say.
Jake Moffatt booked an Air Canada flight after the airline's website chatbot explained a bereavement-fare policy: book now, claim the discount within 90 days.
That version of the policy didn't exist.
Air Canada's real bereavement policy required asking before the flight; the book-now-claim-later part was the bot's invention.
The airline refused to honor it, and argued, in effect, that the chatbot was responsible for its own words.
The British Columbia Civil Resolution Tribunal disagreed and made Air Canada pay: CA$812.02, the fare difference plus interest and fees (Moffatt v.
Air Canada, February 2024).
Note the venue honestly: a provincial small-claims-style tribunal, eight hundred dollars, no grand precedent machinery.
The ruling binds nobody else, and whether any bot statement is legally binding depends on the facts and local law.
The risk-management lesson is still useful: treat every bot statement as something your business may have to answer for.
This book turns that into house policy, not a universal legal theorem: Every promise your tools make becomes your incident to own and resolve.
Nothing unsafe, unlawful, impossible, or above the approved make-good limit gets performed without the Rule 3 escalation.
Chapter 4 warned you when you switched the phones on; this chapter turns the warning into your shop's one-page policy.

One scope line before the rules: this chapter does not cover AI used to make or recommend employment decisions (hiring, firing, scheduling, pay, promotion, discipline, accommodation, or anything like them).
That class needs its own employment-law and human-rights review, with qualified counsel, before any use; nothing on this page clears it.
The other legal fact of machine labor you already know from Chapter 2: the machine gives confidently wrong answers about rules.
New York City's own official business-help chatbot told owners to break laws it existed to explain.
So the two exposure paths are now mapped: what the machine promises outward (your liability to customers) and what the machine tells you inward (compliance advice that's wrong).
One policy page covers both, plus the quiet third exposure most owners never price: what you feed in.
Consumer and business plans can differ by provider, account, region, age, contract, and product surface.
Defaults, menu paths, retention periods, and data-use terms move.

Before real work, open the current first-party documentation for the exact plan and account, record the date and policy version or save a snapshot, and read back which subprocessors are used and what training, retention, sharing, and deletion controls actually apply.
If that direct record is missing or unclear, no live data enters the tool.
A disabled training control is necessary where available, never sufficient: it does not erase retention, provider access, subprocessors, safety review, legal demands, or breach risk.
Live data still needs the clearance below.
After this chapter, you can:
Write the one-page, three-rule AI policy for your shop and get it actually followed
Verify and record the current data-use, retention, sharing, and deletion controls for every exact account your business touches
Keep your tools' promises inside what you'd honor, with the Air Canada test
Answer "is this legal?"
questions the only safe way: from the source of the rule
The primary build: one page, three rules
Long governance documents are for companies with lawyers on payroll.

Yours is one page on the wall, three rules, dated and signed by everyone who touches a work account, you first, and by every new hire before their first login to a work account: day one, not quarter-end.
The three rules answer the three exposures in the order you can control them: what goes in, what goes out, what you believe.
Copy the box below as the wall policy.
The longer rules after it are implementation notes, not extra wall copy.
The one-page policy — print and sign
AI use in this shop
Policy owner: __________  Effective date: __________  Next review: __________
Signed by everyone with a work account: ________________________________
WHAT GOES IN — IF LOSS WOULD REQUIRE AN APOLOGY, STOP.
Use shop-controlled accounts with recorded terms.
Credentials, keys, authentication or recovery codes, and payment or banking secrets never enter an assistant.

Identity, children's, health, employee, tax, legal, insurance, disciplinary, NDA-bound, or restricted data enters only a named controlled workflow whose Appendix B record and qualified sign-off are identified here: __________.
Consumer assistants receive synthetic, sanitized, or non-personal material only.
UNKNOWN, FAIL, or blank means no live connection.
Participants affirmatively agree before recording or transcription.
WHAT GOES OUT — NEW MACHINE WORDS ARE DRAFTS.
A person approves every new or changed customer message.
Only frozen templates and approved substitutions automate after pre-live test and Appendix C rollout.
The system invents no price, deadline, guarantee, policy, remedy, or commitment.
Anything outside the script hands to a person.
If harm reaches someone, stop the workflow, name an incident owner and deadline, contact affected people, deliver the decided remedy, reconcile money, preserve evidence, and fix the script.
Goodwill escalation: Approved internal limit: CA$__________  Authorized owner: __________.
This is not a legal limit.
Anything above it, or involving safety, regulated, contractual, or reliance-sensitive ground, goes to Rule 3.
WHAT WE BELIEVE — RULES COME FROM THE SOURCE OF THE RULE.
No chatbot settles a legal, tax, safety, employment, privacy, accounting, insurance, or compliance question.
Use the controlling primary source and the qualified professional for the decision.
AI may organize questions and documents, but another AI does not make the answer verified.
Disclosure and handoff: Our bot identifies itself as AI and offers the staffed human route during covered hours.
Outside them it uses only the approved no-human script and backup path.
Recording, marketing, accessibility, consumer, workplace, and sector notices require separate local clearance.
Review: Re-read this page quarterly and whenever a tool, plan, purpose, data use, or customer-facing capability changes.
Until the affected workflow is re-cleared, freeze new affected live-data intake and use the tested manual fallback.
Implementation notes for the three rules
RULE 1 — WHAT GOES IN.
Nothing we'd have to apologize for losing.
Consumer assistants receive only synthetic, sanitized, or non-personal material.
An approved business processor receives only the minimum necessary fields after the exact-workflow clearance below.
Credentials, passwords, API keys, authentication codes, recovery secrets, payment or banking secrets, and security configurations never enter any assistant.

Identity documents, children's data, health data, employee records, tax, legal, accounting, insurance, or disciplinary files, trade secrets, source code, unpublished financials, material under an NDA, and other specially regulated or contract-bound material remain out unless a qualified review establishes a separate controlled process.
This list is not exhaustive; uncertainty means stop.
Work uses shop-controlled accounts whose current terms and settings have been recorded.
Meetings require an affirmative yes from every participant before recording or transcription.

Phone-line recording stays off until the exact disclosure/consent flow is documented against official guidance or cleared by a qualified local privacy/compliance professional; stricter contractual, professional, workplace, provincial, or state rules still govern.
Any tool that stores recordings gets its exact plan's data page read before the first meeting: storage, sharing, retention, deletion, and training use.
The test for gray areas: would you pin it to the shop door?
Then it doesn't go in the chat either.
LIVE-DATA CLEARANCE — required before any connection.
The one-page policy does not itself clear live people or business data.

For each exact tool, plan, account, and workflow, complete Appendix B and record evidence, date, and named owner for: operating and data-subject jurisdictions; applicable federal, provincial/state, sector, workplace, health, and contractual rules; minimum necessary fields; purpose and lawful authority or consent; privacy-impact-assessment threshold and result; privacy-officer or qualified-review sign-off where required; vendor/processor agreement; subprocessors; storage and cross-border transfer; data-subject rights; access and security; training/data-use settings; retention and deletion; required notices; breach terms and incident process; export; and the workflow's pre-live test, fallback, and rollback.
Sensitive, regulated, contract-bound, cross-border, or uncertain processing gets qualified local privacy/security advice before connection.
Any blank, uncertain, or failed field means NO LIVE CONNECTION.
A row may be N/A only when the worksheet records the legal or contractual basis for that conclusion, its evidence, date, and owner; N/A is not a substitute for uncertainty.
RULE 2 — WHAT GOES OUT.
Three classes, no ambiguity.
(1) New or changed generated customer language remains a draft until a person reads and approves it; it never earns autonomous promotion.

(2) Fixed, human-approved templates may send automatically only after the Chapter 6 and Chapter 8 gates and the exact Appendix C card pass; approved field substitution is allowed, generated or paraphrased wording is not.

(3) A receptionist may play only exact, deterministic, pre-approved templates and fill pre-approved slots after Chapter 4's phone gates and Appendix C pass, including a technically supported shadow mode.
If the tool cannot support one, customer-facing promotion is prohibited.
Free-form interpretation may only classify intent and select a frozen approved response or slot after the same canonical gate; it may not generate customer-facing wording.
Appendix C is the single authority for event floors, watched periods, controlled-live clocks, promotion, and final decisions; this page adds no shorter route.
Any paraphrase or other new language stays a draft or hands to a person; everything outside the templates and slots hands off.
Every introduced or changed number, date, price, deadline, guarantee, or commitment is source-checked against the controlling record and recalculated where arithmetic applies.
No improvised policies, prices, or guarantees, because of the airline story on the back of this page.
If a tool makes a promise anyway, treat it as an incident: in Moffatt, the misstatement produced a CA$812.02 total award, including damages, interest, and tribunal fees.

The page names the largest make-good we'd honor without a meeting, and that number is internal goodwill and escalation guidance only: never a legal limit, and never a basis to deny what the business actually owes.

Anything above it, and any promise touching regulated, safety, financial, contract, or reliance-sensitive ground, escalates under Rule 3 to a person with the appropriate counsel or adviser in the loop, fast and honest, before anything is acted on.
Escalation is a decision point, not an automatic no: the reviewer decides how to honor, correct, negotiate, or resolve it.
The same day, name the incident owner and deadline, identify and contact every affected customer, deliver the decided remedy, reconcile any money, record evidence of closure, and fix the script.
A vendor fix never closes a customer's incident; the error survived its check, so the task comes back (Chapter 1's firing rule, now company policy).
RULE 3 — WHAT WE BELIEVE.
Rules come from the source of the rule.
No legal, tax, safety, or compliance question gets settled by a chatbot, ours or anyone's; the NYC story is what official-looking wrongness looks like.
The machine may brief the professional (draft our questions, organize our documents); the professional or the primary source decides.

And no AI checks another AI's work and calls it verified: a Texas lawyer tried exactly that, the second tool missed the fabrications, and the court ordered a $2,000 payment to its registry plus mandatory AI education (Chapter 2 carries the case and its record).
Checks run against reality: our documents, our numbers, the actual regulation, a qualified human.
Those are the implementation notes.
The printable box already carries the disclosure, handoff, and review footers; the details here explain how to operate them.

This book's conservative house policy says the bot identifies itself as AI up front and offers the staffed human path during documented coverage hours; outside those hours it uses the fixed no-human script and backup path from Chapter 4.

Recording, telemarketing, consumer-protection, accessibility, and sector-specific notices remain separate jurisdiction-specific gates; the wall sentence does not pretend they are one universal bot-disclosure law.

Re-read the page at the quarterly audit (Chapter 13) and re-check the recorded plan terms and controls with it, because tools and menus change, and a policy that nobody re-reads is a poster, not a policy.

The measured claim, computable as always, and recomputed the way Rule 2 demands: ten minutes of switches, 40 minutes of writing, and five for the bot check — about 55 minutes for Friday's first policy draft.
The separate team talk happens on paid time and is part of the price too; budget fifteen minutes for a small crew, then record what it actually takes.
That under-two-hour block buys the policy shell, not permission to connect live data.

Each exact workflow's Appendix B clearance, vendor-document hunt, account migration, any qualified privacy/security advice, incident investigation, staff training beyond the talk, weekly sampling, and quarterly review are separate recurring or one-time lines to price before launch.
Compare the whole cost with one Moffatt-sized make-good (CA$812, in the real case), one lost client whose data you'd have to confess to pasting, or one afternoon untangling advice a bot invented.
And those are the cheap failures: a leaked health or payment record can carry breach-notification duties and statutory exposure, a number with more digits than any make-good.
The take-backs, named
"The AI said it was legal."
Do not treat that as a defense you can count on.
This book's policy recognizes none, and the machine offers no professional standard or remedy behind the answer; Rule 3 exists so the sentence is never uttered in your shop.
Compliance-by-chatbot.
Minimum wage, tips, scheduling laws, tax thresholds: source-of-rule or professional, every time.
Free answers about laws are priced exactly right.
The unattended bot with a wide script.
Every capability you add to a customer-facing bot is surface area on Rule 2.
Keep the script narrow, keep a person ready to step in, and sample its answers weekly (Chapter 9's ritual).
A bot you can't audit this week is a bot you shouldn't run this week.
Personal accounts for work.
The cheapest data leak there is: work pasted into an account whose settings, retention, and training status you've never seen.
Work uses a shop-controlled account; set available opt-outs, then complete Appendix B before any live data or connection.
An opt-out is one control, never clearance.
Do this Friday
About 60 minutes for Friday's first-pass policy draft and bot check, $0 in tools.
The oldest-chats sweep and the paid team talk are separate scheduled work; migration, investigation, further training, weekly sampling, and the quarterly review also keep their own time.

Tonight, the controls (10 min for the accounts you hold): open the current first-party record for each exact account, record the plan, region, date, and policy version or saved snapshot, and read back the applicable data-use, retention, sharing, and deletion controls.
Screenshot settings pages, not chat contents; those screenshots and policy records are your diligence appendix.
Staff on personal accounts is its own job: this week, ask what each person actually uses and move the work onto shop-controlled accounts, priced in days, not in tonight's ten minutes.
Then scroll your oldest chats once (call it 15 minutes, its own box, outside the 60-minute policy draft): whatever got pasted last year may still be sitting there.
If you find sensitive content, stop.

Freeze further business use and affected integrations; secure the account; revoke shared sessions, links, or tokens as appropriate; name an incident lead the same day; assess connected systems and prior exposure; rotate credentials when compromise is plausible; and invoke the tested manual fallback.
Do not copy, export, or screenshot the payload casually.
Record only necessary metadata — account, date, data category, people affected if known, access, and actions — in the secured incident log.
Preserve content only under the incident lead's or adviser's direction, in controlled storage.

If your organization is subject to PIPEDA, keep the required breach record for 24 months; separately assess whether reporting and notification are required under the real-risk threshold and applicable law.
Delete only what the incident plan or adviser clears.
A customer's card number or health detail is a Rule 3 call now: get qualified privacy help this week, not at the quarterly.
The retention period never delays containment or the call.
Write the page and install the clearance form (40 min): adapt the three rules above in your own words and examples, then copy Appendix B beside it as the required per-tool live-data clearance record.
Every row gets evidence, date, owner, and a pass/no-live decision.
Keep the policy itself to one page even if it hurts; the clearance records sit behind it.
The talk (budget 15 min, schedule it today): walk the page, everyone signs, it goes on the wall and in the drive.

Six staff at the counter often finishes in five, not a conference; solo means you sign it and mean it; a dispersed or shift crew means catching each person once this week, a few minutes each, with the time scaling by headcount, not by this page.
Pair it with Chapter 11's speech only after every Chapter 11 role screen, required private one-to-one, and applicable employment-adviser review is complete.
Otherwise this meeting covers only data-use policy; schedule the headcount talk separately.
The bot audit (5 min, if you run one): read your customer-facing bot's script against Rule 2.
If it could make a promise you would not honor, divert it to the tested manual fallback now.
Edit a non-live copy, rerun the affected Appendix C tests, and resume only after the card owner records the pass.

If a defect may already have reached customers, reconcile the bot log against calls, bookings, complaints, refunds, transfers, and payments; name the owner and deadline, contact affected customers, deliver and reconcile the remedy, and close the incident with evidence.

The takeaway: your business owns what its machines leak, say, and believe — so run one page and three rules: nothing confidential goes in; no new or generated customer wording goes out unread (a frozen approved template still needs the full lifecycle); and rules come from the source of the rule, never the bot.

13.title: The Software Payroll
sentences: Chapter 13
The Software Payroll
Chapter 1 introduced this book's cheapest confession: the author pays five dollars a month to an AI voice tool he hasn't opened in half a year.
Every chapter since has been hiring: a phone answerer, a drafter, a notetaker, a courier.

Which means your business now runs a second payroll, the software payroll, and it has the one property no human payroll could survive: workers who never show up keep getting paid, forever, quietly, by card.
This chapter is the payroll audit, run on a manager's cadence.
It exists because the pattern is universal enough to have a trade name.
Maria Rosey, a PR firm founder, audited her stack and found redundant tools accumulating unnoticed.

Her diagnosis is the whole mechanism in one sentence: "You sign up for a tool during a busy week, you tell yourself it's just for now, then you forget it's even running" (a Forbes contributor piece, Aug 2026; the trade calls it SaaS creep).
Amber de la Garza, a small-business productivity coach, reports finding $5,129 in a two-hour subscription audit.
That's her own account, on her own podcast, so grade it as a practitioner's story, not a study.
The vendor-side numbers point the same way, with two labels on them: they come from subscription-management companies, who profit from you believing this.
And they measure the small and mid-sized companies those vendors serve, which run bigger than ten people.
Read their headline figures (a quarter to thirty percent of spend wasted; roughly a third of seats unused) as directional for your scale, nothing more.
You don't need any of those numbers to be precise.
You need one statement sweep to learn your own.
After this chapter, you can:
Run the quarterly software-payroll audit: every tool lands in Keep, Prove, or Exit
Read your card statement in yearly numbers, the only honest unit for small subscriptions
Cap "keeping up with AI" at two calendar hours a quarter without falling behind
Spot a FOMO ad as Chapter 3's who-profits question in costume, and let it pass without buying
The primary build: two-hour quarterly triage plus variable remediation
Step 1, the sweep (35 min).
Pull thirteen months of every business card and bank account, or a verified recurring-payment report that covers the same window.
Add PayPal and other wallets, app stores, cloud marketplaces, vendor invoices, accounts payable, and employee reimbursements.
That is how annual plans and alternate payment channels make the list instead of hiding outside a three-month window.
Every software line goes on the list, and every monthly price gets multiplied by twelve in the margin, because $19/mo is noise and $228/yr is a decision.
Add separate columns for remediation hours and professional fees: two hours is the triage, not a promise that every repair or exit closes inside it.
(The author's $5 ghost employee is $60/yr; small numbers are how they get you, which is why the yearly column is the audit's only non-negotiable.)
A line you can't identify in ten seconds gets a flag, not a detour: keep sweeping, chase the coded descriptors after, and don't let one mystery charge eat the sweep.
Step 2, the verdicts (40 min).
Every line gets exactly one:
KEEP.
Every AI, automation, newly added, materially changed, or materially risky workflow has its own current probation card (Chapter 10), each metric still clears, and each check still runs.
A generic tool-level card is not enough for those workflows.

Established non-AI infrastructure instead needs one current critical-system record per tool/account: owner, active users, dependencies, authoritative data, access controls, current cost and renewal, backup/restore or reconstruction evidence, continuity path, incident route, and last review.
That record is sufficient under this book unless a new AI/automation use, live-data purpose, material change, or material risk triggers Appendix B and probation.
It enters PROVE only when the record is missing, a trigger appears, or evidence fails; do not freeze ordinary service merely because long-used non-AI infrastructure lacks an AI-workflow card.
At the first audit, an uncarded triggered workflow is PROVE.
Preserve service through the tested manual or human fallback; unproven customer-facing AI returns to watched draft or shadow mode.
Historical records can preserve a phase only when they fill every field and prove that exact current workflow cleared it.

If Appendix B clearance is missing for the triggered workflow, stop new intake and, where safe, pause its ongoing processing, disclosure, scheduled jobs, and affected integrations; preserve evidence and use the tested fallback.

Open the Chapter 12 assessment for potentially affected data and connected systems, contain plausible ongoing exposure, then narrow the response to what the evidence shows was processed; do not freeze unaffected established non-AI service.
Billing hygiene lives here too: downgrade annual-renewing Keeps you over-bought.
Follow Chapter 3's first-year month-to-month rule; after that, compare the annual saving in writing against lock-in and exit risk before prepaying.
PROVE.
You feel it's useful but there's no card and no number, or it is a tool whose metric no longer clears.
It gets a card today (or an updated one) and the applicable Chapter 10 re-probation with real kill criteria.
Feelings don't make payroll; numbers do.
A tool you can't name the job of in one sentence starts here at best, and falls straight through to Exit if it also fails the number and opened-it-lately tests.
Worked once (say, the transcription tool a busy March added): the feeling is real, the card isn't.
Card today, every review date for the correct clock on the calendar.
EXIT.
No job, no number, no opened-it-lately.
Cancellation is the verdict you cannot undo, so the exit gate is objective.

Identify statutory and contractual retention duties; export the authoritative records plus attachments and history; open, count, and sample them; reconcile the final authoritative state; identify the owner, active users, connected systems, recent API or activity logs, and downstream jobs; prove the manual continuity path; and read the renewal terms.
Annual contracts may require advance written notice through a specified channel, and an in-app cancel may not count; read the exact renewal and cancellation clause.
A cheap connector may never be opened and still move booking data every night, so an uncleared dependency stays in Prove.
If the tool held client data, Chapter 12's fence applies on the way out: confirm deletion, backups, legal holds, and subprocessors, not just the export.
A named owner signs off on retention, completeness, operational cutoff, and fallback before cancellation.
Once those checks clear: Cancel today, not "after I check whether we use it" — the audit was the check.
Follow contract terms, provide required notice, complete the in-app flow where applicable, and calendar the effective deadline.
Expect the vendor to fight the leaving harder than it sold the joining: the discount offer, the guilt screen.
Worked once, on the book's own confession: the author's $5 voice tool from Chapter 1 sorts in one breath.
Job it was hired for?
A voice studio nobody has opened in half a year.
Number?
None.
An Exit by the audit's own rules, and if the author hesitates over five dollars, the hesitation is data there too.
And one more column, for any tool that touches customer or client data, whatever its verdict: has its data page changed since you last read it?
Retention, training, sharing.

On the first audit, save a dated PDF or snapshot, or record the vendor's policy-version identifier, plus the key terms: training, sharing, subprocessors, country, retention, deletion, and breach handling.
Every later audit compares against that preserved record, not a mutable URL and a date.
A changed answer moves even a Keep to Prove, because the tool you audited is not the tool it just became.

If the change adds a new use of customer data, immediately freeze new affected live-data intake and integrations, invoke the tested manual fallback, map the affected data and jurisdictions, and compare the change with your privacy notice and preserved record.
Get the required qualified local privacy/security review and re-run Chapter 12 and Appendix B before resuming.
If the change already took effect, assess already-processed data under the incident procedure; later review cannot undo an affected disclosure or retention.
Chapter 12's page is where both live.
Step 3, the policy re-read (10 min).

The one-page AI policy from Chapter 12 (what goes in; why no new or generated customer wording goes out unread while frozen approved templates still need the full lifecycle; where rules come from), out loud if there's a team.
Tools changed this quarter; the page has to have met them.
Step 4, the learning budget (20 min now, capped at two hours a quarter total).
Here is the calm-owner claim, stated plainly: a quarterly cadence is enough, on purpose.
The AI market's churn is spectacular: the directory that counts such things lists some 47,400 AI tools — its own counter, and bigness is its business.
A tracker of dead AI products has logged 106 casualties as of August 2026 (a directional tally), and no trusted, shop-scale Consumer Reports-style authority exists in the retained record.
Those facts point the same way: the noise is the vendors' race, not your homework.
Neither names the right interval, though: quarterly is this book's call, sized to a calendar you'll actually keep, not a finding from any study.

Your two hours: your trade association's take on anything new in your vertical, one practitioner source you trust in your actual trade, and a skim of your kept tools' changelogs for price or data-policy changes (which feed the audit above).
That's it.

The FOMO engine (every "the businesses that adopt X this quarter will bury the ones that don't" ad) is Chapter 3's who-profits question answering itself: anxiety is the product, and the subscription is the treatment being sold.
You are not behind.
You are audited, which is different, and rarer.

It is the thing this book has been building since the first evening: an owner whose tools have jobs, checks, cards, and firing dates is done keeping up, because there is nothing to keep up with except her own numbers.

The measured claim, in your handwriting as always: first-year net audit benefit = avoidable subscription cost actually eliminated during the next twelve months − triage labor − remediation and exit labor − professional fees − cancellation or overlap costs.
Show the ongoing annual run-rate saving separately.
De la Garza's two hours found four figures, by her own account; yours might find a tenth of that, and the arithmetic still works only after your full costs are included.
The book promises no number, and after thirteen chapters you know that's not modesty: numbers you didn't compute yourself don't get believed here, and that includes the book's, and hers.
One last Exit gate before the take-backs: open the export, compare counts, and sample records and their attachments, notes, and history.
Test restore/import where the tool supports it and the state matters; otherwise rehearse a clean-account reconstruction from shop-held prompts, templates, facts, settings, and credential records.
Store a protected backup and have the named owner sign off.
An export button is not an exit path until the result has survived the applicable checks.
The take-backs, named
Daily AI trend news.
Unsubscribe from launch feeds and FOMO roundups.
Keep vendor security, privacy, billing, service-status and shutdown notices, plus alerts from your regulator, insurer, accountant, and trade association; those can demand action today.
A product trend worth buying can wait for the quarterly audit and a track record.
An operational warning cannot.
Mid-quarter impulse hires.
A new tool between audits needs a probation card before the trial, per Chapter 10, or it waits for the audit.
The sketch takes five to ten minutes; its exit and data fields still require separate verification before launch.
The graveyard is built from tools that skipped both during a busy week (Rosey's sentence, laminated).
Annual prepay on anything unproven.
The discount is the vendor pricing your future regret.
Stay monthly through the first year; only after that year, a clean current audit, and a tested exit may annual prepay be considered.
The audit skip.
Miss a quarter and the payroll grows back; the ritual's whole power is that it's boring, scheduled, and shorter than one vendor webinar.
The calendar entry outranks the mood.
Do this Friday
Friday is the first hour of the audit, not a rushed two-hour cancellation spree.

Use 35 minutes to sweep and 25 minutes to begin verdicts; complex exports, cancellations, contract notice, dependency tracing, remaining verdicts, and card work get their own scheduled follow-up blocks.
Sweep every payment channel (35 min) across thirteen months (or a verified recurring-payment report with the same reach), list every software line, write the ×12 column.
Begin the verdicts (25 min): Keep / Prove / Exit.
Say each tool's one-sentence job out loud; hesitation is data.
Stop at the hour and schedule the unfinished rows.
For a tool only a teammate uses, get their sentence before you verdict: the dispatcher's answer counts, not your guess at it.

Schedule the Exits: reserve a follow-up block with enough time to open, count, and sample the export; test restore/import where supported and material, or rehearse the clean-account reconstruction; back up; and obtain named-owner sign-off before cancellation.
In that block, follow contract terms, provide required written notice, complete the in-app cancellation flow where applicable, and calendar the effective deadline.
Expect the cancel-flow gauntlet (the discount offer, the guilt screen); your card on file was the product, and leaving is usually the feature they made hardest.
Schedule the Proves.
Reserve a separate follow-up block for each Chapter 10 probation card and day-30 review; the five card fields and their exit/data proof do not fit inside Friday's first hour.
Calendar next quarter's triage (two hours, thirteen weeks out), the separate two-hour learning budget, and every remediation block your hours-and-fees columns exposed.
Then close the laptop only after each open repair has an owner and date.
The cadence is enough to find the work; the repair time is measured separately.

The takeaway: your tools are a payroll — audit it quarterly into Keep, Prove, or Exit with yearly numbers, cap the keeping-up at two hours a quarter, and let the market churn without you; calm is what an audited stack feels like.

Read their headline figures (a quarter to thirty percent of spend wasted; roughly a third of seats unused) as directional for your scale, nothing more.

An export button is not an exit path until the result has survived the applicable checks. The take-backs, named Daily AI trend news. Unsubscribe from launch feeds and FOMO roundups. Keep vendor security, privacy, billing, service-status and shutdown notices, plus alerts from your regulator, insurer, accountant, and trade association; those can demand action today. A product trend worth buying can wait for the quarterly audit and a track record. An operational warning cannot. Mid-quarter impulse hires. A new tool between audits needs a probation card before the trial, per Chapter 10, or it waits for the audit. The sketch takes five to ten minutes; its exit and data fields still require separate verification before launch. The graveyard is built from tools that skipped both during a busy week (Rosey's sentence, laminated). Annual prepay on anything unproven.

The discount is the vendor pricing your future regret. Stay monthly through the first year; only after that year, a clean current audit, and a tested exit may annual prepay be considered. The audit skip. Miss a quarter and the payroll grows back; the ritual's whole power is that it's boring, scheduled, and shorter than one vendor webinar. The calendar entry outranks the mood. Do this Friday Friday is the first hour of the audit, not a rushed two-hour cancellation spree. Use 35 minutes to sweep and 25 minutes to begin verdicts; complex exports, cancellations, contract notice, dependency tracing, remaining verdicts, and card work get their own scheduled follow-up blocks. Sweep every payment channel (35 min) across thirteen months (or a verified recurring-payment report with the same reach), list every software line, write the ×12 column. Begin the verdicts (25 min): Keep / Prove / Exit.

Say each tool's one-sentence job out loud; hesitation is data. Stop at the hour and schedule the unfinished rows. For a tool only a teammate uses, get their sentence before you verdict: the dispatcher's answer counts, not your guess at it. Schedule the Exits: reserve a follow-up block with enough time to open, count, and sample the export; test restore/import where supported and material, or rehearse the clean-account reconstruction; back up; and obtain named-owner sign-off before cancellation. In that block, follow contract terms, provide required written notice, complete the in-app cancellation flow where applicable, and calendar the effective deadline. Expect the cancel-flow gauntlet (the discount offer, the guilt screen); your card on file was the product, and leaving is usually the feature they made hardest. Schedule the Proves.

14.title: Your Next Twelve Months
sentences: Chapter 14
Your Next Twelve Months
Thirteen chapters ago you were at the counter after close, wondering whether a machine could do the last job of the day and how you'd know if it did it wrong.
You now hold the answers as working equipment: two questions, a failure map, named checks, probation cards, a policy page, an audited payroll.
This last chapter is about time: what the next year of this looks like, what changes underneath you, and what doesn't.
After this chapter, you can:
Place every tool you run on the three-rung ladder and know what check each rung demands
Read the four signals of a dying tool and act before the shutdown email
Decide switch-versus-sit with one rule: switch on your numbers, sit on the market's
Write the one-page plan that turns this book into your next twelve months
The ladder: assistant, automations, agents
Machine labor comes in three rungs of independence, and the book has been walking you up them in order.
Rung one: the assistant.
Work happens when you ask, one task at a time, checked as it lands.
The drafting, summarizing, and analysis work in Chapters 4 through 7 lives here.
In this book's judgment, most businesses should spend most of their first year on rung one, and a year there is not slow; it is how the checking habits form while the stakes are small.
Rung two: automations.
Work happens on triggers without your hands (Chapter 8's couriers), but each deterministic trigger, transfer, and fixed-template step follows a recipe you wrote.
The failure shape is repetition and the check is the run log.

Appendix C is the single authority for its adversarial tests, shadow evidence, customer-facing watched period, controlled-live probation, and final decision; generated or paraphrased customer language never earns autonomous promotion.
A hybrid workflow is graded by its riskiest component, inheriting rung one's invention and misreading checks as well as rung two's run controls.
A transfer bot and an open-ended AI receptionist are not the same hire.
Rung three: agents.
Software that plans multi-step work on its own: reads the inbox, decides what matters, acts, remembers.
This rung is real, and this book's honest report is that at owner scale it is early.
One secondhand account at anything like your size describes Scott Bell, a solo bankruptcy lawyer, running a small fleet of open-source agents on OpenClaw.

The reported arc reads like a trust ladder: months of specifying "every teensy step," an orchestrator taking notes, and only then delegated judgment such as flagging court notices and drafting reply ideas.
Nobody interviewed his clients, audited an agent's decision, or resolved the professional-supervision question.
It is unverified context, not evidence that the approach is safe or effective.
The same platform's public record that season includes reported inbox deletion despite stop commands and fabricated board figures (TechCrunch, Feb 2026; Business Insider, Mar 2026).
The rung-three verdict by the book's own instrument: agents concentrate exactly what Chapter 1 taught you to price.
Wide blast radius, expensive verification.
So they inherit the strictest version of every rule, not a waiver.

If you climb in year one: one agent, one read-only job on copies; least-privilege credentials; no send, delete, edit, or other outside effect without approval for that action; a tested stop control; a verified backup and rollback; no money movement or unsupervised customer contact; probation doubled from Chapter 10's standard 30 days to 60; run logs read weekly.
An agent may prepare a purchase packet or cart only.
A human independently opens the first-party payment interface, verifies vendor, amount, destination, and terms, and executes the purchase; no standing approval exists.
Human approval tests only that exact non-purchase action, not a wider privilege, and any new action or permission restarts the gate and 60-day clock.
If the tool cannot meet that fence, wait.
Rungs one and two carry every checkable win this book teaches, your own probation cards will tell you what they returned, and rung three will still be there once it has a track record.

One contrast case, for calibrated ambition rather than fever: Base44, launched by a single founder in January 2025, was acquired by Wix that June, five months in, for a reported $80 million upfront (TechCrunch, Jun 2025).
The revenue and profit figures along the way were the founder's own, unaudited.
The sources document nothing about his verification process, so no moral about "judgment" gets to ride on it.
It happened; it is not a plan.
The plan is the boring ladder, climbed at the speed of your checks.
Signals a tool is dying, and the switch/sit rule
Tools die; a tracker exists just to log AI products that didn't make it.
You don't need to predict failures, only to notice the four signals early:
The changelog goes quiet: no updates in two quarters while the category moves.
Price hikes arrive with nothing attached: monetizing the trapped.
Support you once had degrades to a bot with no human path: a vendor that removes its human lane has stopped investing in keeping you.
(A tool that was always bot-first gets judged on the other three.)
The data-export door narrows: exit risk has increased, whatever the vendor's reason.
One hard signal — an export restriction, shutdown notice, security or privacy deterioration, or loss of critical support — triggers the contingency plan.

For security or privacy deterioration, freeze new live-data intake and affected integrations immediately, invoke the tested manual fallback, name the incident owner, assess prior exposure, and require full Chapter 12 re-clearance before resuming.
Export safely under the incident plan rather than widening exposure.
For the other hard signals, run the tested export while it still works.
Any two softer signals together (a starting rule, not a statute) move the tool to Prove at the next audit.

If the tool held customer data, ask the vendor to confirm in writing what was deleted, when, which backups or legal holds remain, what subprocessors retain, and whether any past model training can be reversed.
And the switch/sit rule for the shinier direction, new tools: switch on your numbers, sit on the market's.
Your probation card's metric sagging, your checks catching more, your audit finding a better-fitting Keep: switch.
A launch video, a competitor's ad, a headline about the model that changes everything: sit.
Chapter 13 already capped your exposure to the second kind at two hours a quarter; this rule is what those hours are for.
The market will re-run its entire drama annually.
Your instrument is built to outlast that churn, because it was never about the tools: two questions, checks that fit failure shapes, probation, a policy page, an audit.
None of those names a vendor, which is why a model release can't retire them, and why they, and not a tool list, are what this book asked you to learn.
The one-page plan

Before any rung-three trial appears on this plan, pass one admission gate: a named operating need cannot be met on rungs one or two, and the relevant lower-rung cards and checks have stayed healthy for at least one clean quarter.
Otherwise, stay lower.
Write it Friday and review it quarterly.
Revise sooner after a failed check, incident, staff or ownership change, vendor-policy change, or new legal or data duty.
Five lines:

This quarter's one hire: the single workflow from your pain chapter (the one you flipped to first), on a probation card — Chapter 10's index card: one job, one metric with a baseline, named checks, kill criteria, exit path.

A filled first line reads (labeled illustration): "Q4: after-hours phone answering (it announces itself as an assistant; recording stays off until the documented consent flow is cleared), carded: qualified booking rate vs the call log's baseline; deterministic transfer plus fixed-template intake using approved minimum-necessary fields and pre-approved slots; no diagnosis, negotiation, new promises, or money movement; immediate human escalation outside script; next-morning callbacks confirm the first month's bookings, then Monday-and-Thursday call-listens; gone unless it beats baseline after the prewritten minimum sample, extended once if the month ran too quiet to judge; export path confirmed."
The deterministic transfer follows rung two.

Any free-form interpretation or generated customer-facing language inherits the highest applicable controls from Chapters 1, 2, 4, 8, and 10; if open-ended judgment is needed, the workflow must hand off to a human.
The standing checks: your named check per delegated task, the weekly review during any probation, the quarterly audit.
Three habits; everything else in this book hangs off them.

The never-list: your take-backs, written where you'll re-read them: can't-verify work, can't-survive work, money movement, compliance-by-chatbot (those questions go to your accountant or lawyer, not a text box), and whatever your trade adds.

The team sentence: Chapter 11's present-intent statement, kept in writing: capacity is the design; no reduction is currently planned because of this rollout; if plans change, they hear it from you first, directly and lawfully.
Next quarter's maybe: the one tool or rung you'll consider then, parked by name, so ads have nothing to sell you in between.
The last scene
Picture one hypothetical Tuesday, if the checks have held.
The phone answers itself politely at 9 p.m. (it identifies itself; any recording runs only under the documented consent flow) and books the job.
The quote goes out with a total you re-added in nine seconds.

The follow-up sends because it was Tuesday, to a customer who said yes to hearing from you, opt-out line riding along; the books skim clean over one coffee a month, and a reply you drafted-then-humanized to a customer's review brings a stranger to the counter.
None of it is dramatic; that was the point all along.
Somewhere in there is the evening this book cost you, paid back weekly, and a machine that never became your partner, your oracle, or your replacement.
It became what you hired on page one, once you knew what you were hiring: the strangest employee you'll ever manage, working under the oldest rules you know.
Your judgment did this.
It was never the thing being replaced.
It was the thing being aimed, and it is aimed now.
Close the book.
The shop is yours, a little more than it was.

The takeaway: climb the ladder at the speed of your checks — assistant, then automations, then maybe agents — act immediately on a hard signal, flag two soft signals now for Prove at the next audit, switch on your numbers and sit on the market's, and run the five-line plan; the instrument you built is the part built to last.

pending.text: Why careful owners collect dead subscriptions Fear signs up. The headlines say most businesses already use AI, and a directory now lists some 47,400 tools to feel behind about. No independent body reviews any of them. The numbers are softer than they look. When BDC, Canada's bank for entrepreneurs, asked owners whether they used AI, 39% said yes. Shown examples first, 66% said yes. The answer depends on the question. And when statistics agencies count businesses actually running AI in their operations, they find 8.8% in the United States and 19.2% in Canada (US Census, 2025; Statistics Canada, 2026). You are not behind. The feeling that you are is manufactured, and it is profitable. The calendar keeps. Rosey named the mechanism: the busy week. Novelty and a deadline start the trial; auto-renewal converts "just for now" into a default. Canceling requires a decision.

Renewing requires nothing. Vendors understand that asymmetry, which is why trials collect a card number first. Guilt defends. By month three, the tool has cost setup hours and real dollars. Canceling feels like admitting the waste, so "we should really use it more" becomes the plan. And because no one owns the tool, no one ever has to deliver a verdict. Keeping it feels thrifty; it is the only option that costs money every single month. Economists call this the sunk-cost trap. The graveyard runs on it. Fear signs up, the calendar keeps, guilt defends. That is the whole machine, and every part of it stops the moment a tool has a task, an owner, and a number. You install those three in the next ten minutes of reading. The Noise Test Before believing any tool's promise, including the ones in this book, ask one question: Who profits from me believing I need this now?

Verdict math: $138 a month walks out the door — $1,656 a year back in yours. $30 stays and earns. $30 gets a 30-day deadline instead of another year of guilt. Notice why each tool died. The writing tool fell to overlap: a wide, cheap generalist covers it, which is why a specialist must earn its seat after the $20 tool fails at something valuable. The SEO tool fell to a missing task. Nothing fell to being "bad software." Before canceling anything, protect the exit: export your work, and check whether a form, calendar, or customer message runs through the tool. Expect the cancel screen to fight back: a 50%-off retention offer, a warning that your data will be deleted. That is the graveyard defending itself. Export first, decline twice. Then cancel on evidence, not guilt.

And this is not theoretical bookkeeping: Amber de la Garza, a small-business productivity coach, says one two-hour audit found her $5,129 in canceled subscriptions, downgrades, and renegotiated contracts, by her own account on her own podcast; she didn't publish how much of it recurs yearly. Her audit ran long because she renegotiated on the spot. Yours, below, just sorts and totals — the exits can wait for Saturday. A cheap tool without a weekly job is expensive. Two risks worth ten minutes Tools die young. AI tools are mostly young companies running on borrowed money, and young companies fold, pivot, and get acquired; one hobbyist tracker has logged 106 confirmed shutdowns, and nobody counts the full toll. The insurance costs a few dollars: month-to-month billing usually runs higher than the annual plan, by vendor design — pay the difference for any tool under a year old anyway.

It is the cheapest insurance in this book. Export your data quarterly, and never let one tool be the only place customer information lives. Chapter 3 prices exits properly. Your team is already using AI. MIT researchers found in 2025 that at more than 90% of companies studied, employees used personal AI accounts at work. Ask your people what they already paste into free chatbots (customer emails? the price list?) because nobody vetted where that text goes. The answer closes a data hole and hands you a free list of tools worth piloting on purpose. Chapter 12 turns this into a one-page policy. Do this Friday Total time: about 47 minutes, in pieces. Can't wait for Friday? Do step 1 tonight — it's five minutes, and the bank app is already in your hand. Pull three months of charges (5 min). Search your business card and bank statements for software and app-store payments. Cancel nothing yet.

Build a one-page list (15 min). For each tool: monthly cost, its one task, its owner, the last date it produced something useful. Mark each line (10 min). Keep means task, owner, and proof are all present. Prove means unsure. Exit means no task or no owner. Protect the exits (10 min). Export data, check what breaks, then cancel — through the retention offers, twice. If a tool touches customers, payments, or your website, schedule the safe exit rather than rushing it. Set one proof test (5 min). Each Prove tool gets 30 days, one measurable result, and a calendar date. No new tools during the test. Total the stack (2 min). Monthly charges × 12, posted where you will see it before the next free trial. What you just bought back Run the audit and you own something rare: a statement you can explain, line by line, before it arrives.

If your shelf looks anything like this chapter's, you also freed real money: $138 a month is $1,656 a year, about a month of a part-timer's wages. You bought it with 47 minutes and zero new software, and the couch hour goes back to being yours. You'll run the rest of this book the same way, one function at a time, with real prices and the catch always stated. But before you buy anything new, there's a problem: the tools you'll evaluate can lie to you — fluently, confidently, and in perfect grammar. Chapter 2 shows you exactly when to trust AI and when it's bluffing, because the next mistake on the menu is more expensive than $200 a month. The takeaway: do not pay for AI because it is impressive; pay only when a named task, a named owner, and a number prove it belongs in your business.

Chapter 2 The Worker's Failure Map Chapter 1 left you with two questions (can you check the work at a glance, and could you survive the worst version?). This chapter widens them into four separate decisions, made in order, every time you hand work over. Zero-th, clearance: are this data and this call yours to give a machine at all? Consumer assistants get synthetic, sanitized, or non-personal material only. An approved business processor may receive minimum-necessary live data only after Chapter 12 clears the exact tool, plan, account, workflow, and jurisdiction. Credentials, payment secrets, authentication codes, specially regulated material, and any authority you do not hold remain hard stops. First, the check: is there a check that runs against reality, and will you actually run it?

Ask for court cases and it can give you court cases: correctly formatted, persuasively named, and sometimes nonexistent. Amir Mostafavi, a California employment lawyer running his own practice, filed an appeals brief in which 21 of 23 quotations turned out to be fabricated by the AI tools he'd used. The court sanctioned him $10,000, reported at the time as the largest such sanction in the state, and published its opinion as a warning to the profession (Noland v. Land of the Free, September 2025; court record). Note what his story adds to Karlen's from Chapter 1: Karlen was a business owner who couldn't check legal work. Mostafavi is a lawyer. The gap-filling failure got them both, because catching an invented citation requires checking every citation, and the polish gives you no reason to.

The tell that isn't there: invented material can sound just as confident and specific as real material. Fluency does not reveal which one you are reading. 2. It drops things silently. Ask it to summarize, merge, or clean, and the recurring result in this book's logged runs was most of it right and one piece quietly lost. This book ran its own bounded trials: six owner-sized tasks, each run through two configurations, A and B, every output checked against the source. The records do not form public product-grade or price-tier evidence. Worker A's supplier-terms summary dropped one payment condition; its contact-list cleanup merged two duplicates and silently lost a note attached to one of them. No error message. No "I skipped something." The output looks complete because completeness is a look. A person who loses a piece of your paperwork usually knows they lost it.

This is the least dangerous family because it's the most visible, and it is the reminder the others need: the worker is assembling patterns, not remembering you. Which leads to the fifth shape, the one that owners find hardest to believe. 5. It doesn't reliably stay corrected. This one is different in kind: shapes 1 through 4 are ways a task's output fails, while shape 5 is a standing property of the worker, and it governs every task you delegate. Context, saved memory, retrieval, and customization may influence a later run; none guarantees that Tuesday's correction governs Thursday's answer. So treat every correction as a correction to the draft until a written rule and a new check prove otherwise.

The practical consequence is a habit: anything you find yourself correcting twice goes into your controlled instructions, script, or facts sheet, because the record is inspectable even when the model's behavior is not. If more than one person uses the tool, that record needs access control and one named owner; otherwise shape 5 just moves into separate chat histories. After this chapter, you can: Run the four delegation decisions in order (clearance, check, survivability, payoff) before any handoff Name the five failure shapes and say which one a given task invites Match each of your delegated tasks to the check that catches its shape Explain why "are you sure?" and AI-checking-AI are not verification Write the first rows of your own failure map, with a take-back line The map: task families and the checks that fit them

The reason Chapter 1's named checks work is that each one is aimed at a failure shape. Read them as minimum checks: each cuts the risk of its shape, none removes it, and a check can miss, which is what the last column prices. Where a check says compare, it means compare against the original you hold, knowing what you expected to change; a difference you didn't expect is a finding, not a formatting choice. Here is the whole instrument on one page, built from the six task families in this book's logged trials and the shapes above: Task family The failure it invites The minimum check that cuts the risk If the check fails you Drafts you'll send (replies, emails) template leakage; tone off

One machine's confident guess does not become verification because a second machine agreed; the lesson of his case is the book's rule: checks run against reality (your documents, your numbers, the source of the rule) or they are not checks. And notice who this book's lawyer stories are about: small firms and solo practices, chosen because they are your scale, not because big firms are immune. The record repeats at that scale. Chong Ke, at a small Vancouver family-law firm, was ordered to personally pay for the time wasted on two invented cases she had filed (CBC, February 2024; the first reported Canadian instance). And one honest note about the pile: its one business owner is Chapter 1's Jonathan Karlen; nearly every other name is a lawyer, not because lawyers are careless, but because courts publish their failures. Your trade's version doesn't make the paper; it just makes a bad week.

That is why this book ran its own logged trials on owner-sized tasks instead of waiting for your case file. Mostafavi, Monk, and Ke are not stupid people. They are busy people in checkable-looking situations where the checking was the whole job, and the polish said it was already done. Your week contains the same trap at smaller stakes, which is the only reason this chapter exists. What this means for the leash Chapter 1 gave you three firing rules (its two questions screened what to hand over; the firing rules govern taking work back). The map refines the leash they tug: Shape 1 tasks (invention risk) get delegated only with a source attached: the facts sheet, the price list, the policy document, plus the standing instruction if it isn't in the source, say so instead of answering.

And whether a consumer tool trains on your conversations is not one fact: it varies by vendor, product, plan, account type, region, mode, and settings, and vendors revise it, so treat your tool's answer as unknown until you have checked it (the chapter note carries what this book verified, with dates; Chapter 12 carries the switches and the full fence). A training toggle turned off is not permission to paste sensitive data. Shape 3 tasks (misreading) stay behind the line from Chapter 1. The map adds the why: the check for a misreading requires the expertise the delegation was meant to replace. There is no discipline that fixes a circular check. There is only not delegating it.

Shape 5 (no reliable staying power) is not a task family but a property of the worker, and it sets your management style: instructions live in controlled documents, not in an assumption that the worker learned from being told.

Give each a row, and run the four decisions on it: does its data clear the zero-th gate (consumer assistants get synthetic, sanitized, or non-personal data only; live data waits for the exact business-workflow clearance in Chapter 12); which task family above; which failure shape it invites; which minimum check catches that shape; what the worst survivable version costs; and does the payoff hold, meaning the time the task saves beats the time its check takes. (One worked as a model: "reply to the Tuesday review," the friendly one, is a draft you'll send; it invites template leakage and tone slips; the check is reading it before it sends; the worst survivable version costs an apology, and it clears the first row's boundary: no money, no promise, no complaint, no employee, nothing sensitive in it. The angry review is a complaint, which crosses that boundary and leaves the row.)

For your best delegation candidate, assemble its facts sheet once: prices, policies, the three answers you always give (build it only from data that clears the zero-th gate: prices, policies, stock answers, never live customer or employee details; whether a consumer tier trains on conversations varies by vendor, plan, and settings, a training toggle turned off is not permission, and Chapter 12 carries the switches and the full fence). Ten minutes now; it gives shape 1 fewer places to hide on every future run of that task. Your map will have five tasks, and a few more rows where they split. The book's map has six families. Growth is adding rows, not trust.

The takeaway: the machine's failures have shapes — invention, silent loss, authoritative misreading, template leakage, and no reliable learning from your corrections — and a delegation is safe only when its shape has a check you'll actually run.

The final order, approved unanimously in January 2025, added a separate requirement: DoNotPay had to tell its own past subscribers about the settlement. Notice what the FTC did not say. It did not say AI cannot help with legal paperwork. It said DoNotPay had not substantiated its advertised human-lawyer equivalence through the testing the FTC required. The marketing claim, eventually, met a check. That enforcement action made DoNotPay one of the most scrutinized AI products in America. The tens of thousands of other tools on the market have faced less. There is no Consumer Reports for AI, and the regulator shows up occasionally, after the damage. Nobody is coming to review the tool you are about to buy. So the review has to be yours, and short enough that you will actually run it. This chapter is that review: five questions, one index card, about thirty minutes.

The filter is distilled from three sources that take the problem seriously: the Small Business Administration's vendor checklists, the AI Risk Management Framework from NIST (the federal standards body), and MIT's research on why AI pilots fail. You get the five questions that survive translation into plain English. Think of this as the job interview for Chapter 1's strangest employee, and start with the question that decides whether a candidate even gets the interview. The incentive check: who profits from me believing this? Every claim that reaches you arrived on someone's payroll. The vendor profits if you believe the demo. The affiliate reviewer profits if you click their "honest comparison" (Chapter 5 explains why affiliate programs multiply product lists). The course seller profits if you feel behind.

The kept tools produced a measurable result inside a real workflow, inside a defined window. The merely impressive got dropped. Every ten missed calls is ten conversations you never had, five jobs you never won, $1,500 that went to a competitor whose phone got answered. That range is vendor math, so treat it as directional; the per-call arithmetic above, done on your own log, is the number that counts. (If your work is retainer clients rather than inbound quote calls, your leak lives in Chapter 6's quiet threads, not the acquisition ring count.) Meanwhile, most owners trying to "do AI" are generating social media posts. Marketing pours water into the top of a leaky bucket. This chapter plugs the hole in the bottom. The order matters: capture the demand you already have before you spend a dollar creating more. Why speed is the whole game

For decades the options were an answering service, a hired dispatcher, or your own interrupted evening. AI adds another option: software that can answer after hours at a variable subscription and usage cost, plus setup, integration, clearance, checking, and fallback labor. Your quote and probation record — not the price of one job — decide whether it pays. Owners who set this up describe the same two results. First, booked work they would have missed. Second, and they mention this almost as often: the phone stops owning them. Dinner is dinner. That second result is why this book keeps insisting AI's best gift to a small business is not headcount math. It is getting pieces of your life back: capacity and relief, never a promise about cutting people. What "answering" needs to include An AI receptionist that just takes messages is voicemail with better manners.

A useful setup may support four steps in a row, but each step has its own clearance and evidence burden. Think of it as one pipeline: answer → book → follow up → ask for the review. Cover every call without pretending a human is always awake. During documented staffed hours, the system may use frozen answers and transfer within the written acknowledgment limit. Outside them, it may capture a message or make a deterministic low-risk booking only. Complaints may receive the fixed no-human-available message and a truthful callback window. Safety, emergency, medical, legal, allergy, medication, regulated, uncertain, and human-request calls do not enter that ordinary callback class: they receive only the trade- and jurisdiction-specific approved notice and staffed route written for that class. If you cannot staff and test the route, the bot does not handle the exception.

Book straight into your calendar. Not "someone will call you back." The caller hangs up holding a time slot. G.L. Hunt, a family-owned Texas foundation-repair company, reports a 40% higher booking rate after wiring AI follow-up into its missed-call handling. That number comes from Hatch, its software vendor, so treat it as a best case. The math that matters is smaller and yours: current subscription and usage, setup and integration hours, and weekly audit-and-check labor, totaled over a stated period (a quarter is fair). The business case is one line: the margin on booked jobs your own log says you were losing must beat that all-in cost. Follow up automatically — only after the channel is cleared. Missed a call anyway? A person may want to send: "Sorry we missed you — want to book a time or tell us what you need?" Do not infer automated-message permission from the missed inbound call.

Record the exact message, purpose, relationship, dates, evidence, sender identification, and unsubscribe requirement in Appendix B; qualified communications/privacy counsel signs the applicable legal-classification rows, and the technical reviewer signs the controls. A direct response to a request or complaint is not treated here as a marketing sequence, but any uncertainty keeps automation off and defaults to a manual callback. Ask for the review. Job done, the system requests a Google review and drafts your reply. Reviews feed the next customer's decision, which feeds the phone, which is the whole loop. This book's conservative house rule puts an electronic review request through the same lawful-basis, sender-identification, proof, and unsubscribe checks as the follow-up above; exact duties vary by channel and jurisdiction, so confirm yours.

If you cannot document the basis and controls, ask manually or put a neutral review link on the receipt. The same house rule sends the ask to everyone or no one — never screen out unhappy customers first — and waits until the job is actually settled, with no open complaint or callback and repeat customers asked at most a few times a year. Confirm the current platform and regulator rules before automating the ask. Restaurants run the same play with orders instead of appointments. Little Italy, an independent restaurant, put an AI agent on its phone line connected to its Toast register and went live in three days (the vendor, Loman, tells the story, same caveat as above). The retained record does not provide enough metric detail to print the vendor's labor-cost percentage, and the story does not independently establish call coverage or service quality.

What stays human, and the check that keeps it honest Two call classes get taken back before any tool goes live, in writing, in the script. The setup names that person: whose phone the urgent flag lands on, and the longest a flag may wait before a second person picks it up. Three warnings before you switch anything on Treat your AI's promises as promises you may have to answer for. In 2024 a British Columbia small-claims-style tribunal awarded a customer damages after Air Canada's chatbot described a bereavement discount wrongly: the airline's real policy required asking before the flight, and the book-now-claim-later version the bot offered didn't exist. The ruling binds nobody else, and legal effect depends on the facts and local law. The risk lesson is still useful, so this book adopts it as house policy. Keep your AI's script narrow.

It should answer the questions you gave it, book only approved appointments, and say "I'll have someone confirm that" for every non-safety, non-complaint, out-of-scope request. Safety and emergency language follows only the separately approved route above. Never let it improvise prices, guarantees, or availability you didn't write down. Chapter 12 goes deeper. Say it's an AI up front, clear the applicable rows, and staff the handoff. Have the bot introduce itself as an assistant instead of waiting to be asked. Identification, recording, transcription, notice, consent, jurisdiction, and sector duties vary by place and use. Before launch, complete Appendix B: counsel signs the applicable legal rows, a qualified privacy/security practitioner signs the technical and operational rows, and any blank or UNKNOWN keeps the flow off.

Some callers will want a human: a message, an urgent flag, and a person who actually sees it. An AI receptionist with no human backstop is how you miss the one call that mattered while feeling covered. Know where the recordings live. A phone AI processes callers' audio and may record and/or transcribe it; callers blurt things they would only tell you: the panicked tax question, the address, the medical detail. Before switch-on, read the tool's data page (where calls and transcripts are stored, for how long, whether they train models). Chapter 6 handles what happens after someone responds. The three delegations you never make here 1. Pictures of what you sell. A product photo is a promise about the physical world. (The full weekly loop runs three events in about 30 minutes; today is the small first rep.) Set the boundary in writing: add to the Pack: "No AI images of products or premises. Chapter 6 Follow-Up You Won't Forget Somewhere in your sent folder is a quote from three weeks ago that never got an answer. You meant to follow up. Then Thursday happened, and following up started to feel like pestering, and now it feels too late. (Labeled illustration, but check your sent folder before you call it hypothetical.) Here are the plain mechanics of the leak: follow-up doesn't die of skill. You know exactly what to say to the customer who went quiet; you'd say it perfectly if they walked in. Follow-up dies of memory and mood: remembering on the right day, and feeling like it isn't begging. Which makes this domain almost comically well-suited to the strangest employee you'll ever hire, because the machine has no Thursday and no pride. It never forgets the day, and it never feels awkward.

Name the follow-up delegations you never make: deal changes, cold blasts, and endless sequences Count your own leak in quotes-without-answers, this Friday, from your sent folder The primary build: the two-touch thread One paper sheet, already-cleared shop system, or locally controlled file; one calendar; the assistant you have. A new cloud spreadsheet or notes account must pass Appendix B before any live name, quote fact, or contact detail enters it. Zero new dollars to start. 1. Capture: the thread list. One line per open lead: name, what was quoted, date sent, next-touch date, eligible/not eligible, reply, booked/won/lost, lost reason if known, unsubscribe, and complaint. Ten seconds at the moment you send any quote, then one result mark when the thread ends. This list IS your CRM for now; the discipline of writing the line is the habit every failed CRM purchase was trying to buy. 2.

Touch one, day 3: the useful nudge. Not "just checking in." Until Chapter 12's live-data gate has cleared the drafting tool, build the reusable message with placeholders such as [FIRST NAME], [JOB DETAIL], and [DATE], then fill them locally from the quote and calendar. A sendable shape to copy: "Measured your gutters against the quote from Tuesday — the 40-foot run is why the number looks high. Happy to walk you through it, and next week's install slots are open Thursday and Friday." You read it once against the two checks that matter: is everything in it true, and would you say it across the counter? If the draft introduced a fact or changed any fact you gave it (the measurement, the price, the slot), it goes back for a source check against the quote and the calendar before anything sends.

Before either touch goes live, confirm the lawful basis or consent for that channel, keep the proof, identify the sender, and include the unsubscribe control your rule requires; if you cannot document the basis, do not send. Rules differ by country, so check yours. Send only after those gates pass. 3. Touch two, day 10: the honest close. The machine drafts the version you'd never quite write yourself because it feels too direct: "Wanted to close the loop on the quote from the 4th. If the timing's wrong or you went another way, no hard feelings; if you'd like to proceed, I can confirm current availability." Use the same placeholders and channel-compliance gate as touch one. Promise a hold only when the authoritative calendar contains a real customer-specific reservation with a tested expiry and release. True dates only. Send. 4. Stop.

Two touches, then the lead moves to a "later" list that gets one seasonal note, ever. One consent check comes before that note: a past customer is not permanent permission. Classify the message before it leaves. A direct response to a request or complaint is not treated here as a marketing sequence. A promotional note needs express consent or a qualifying relationship or inquiry whose exact dates and current statutory criteria you have documented. If the category, evidence, jurisdiction, or clock is unclear, the system stays off and a qualified person decides. Every permitted note names the sender, carries a working unsubscribe, and keeps the proof of its basis. That stop is written policy. It protects the asset every follow-up spends a little of: being someone whose messages people open.

One lane may run longer when you are chasing documents, signatures, or statements needed to complete an agreed transaction, but do not assume that makes the electronic message exempt. Classify the exact template, channel, relationship, and transaction against current CASL section 6 and CRTC guidance or qualified Canadian advice; sender-identification and unsubscribe duties may still apply. If uncertain, keep the automated message off. Return the call only if the exact call is permitted under current calling rules or qualified local advice; otherwise keep the workflow paused. When cleared, the written edge is weekly, four times, then a permitted person-to-person call; the machine never sends a fifth. 5. The schedule link. If your business books time, put a scheduling link in both touches.

Calendly is one example; record the current first-party plan, event-type limit, seats, reminders, payment features, tax, currency, and billing period before choosing it. Chapter 3 keeps you on free or monthly billing through year one. Skip it if jobs need a site visit before any booking is real: a link that books unquotable work manufactures awkward calls. The measured claim, yours to compute: count last month's eligible quotes and estimates that got no reply and no follow-up (Friday's step 1 turns this same count into a working list). Multiply that count by your estimated follow-up response rate, then by your historical close rate after a response, then by contribution margin per job, not full revenue. Until your thread list supplies a local response rate, run a low and high scenario and label it an assumption.

The result is scenario recoverable contribution margin, not the pipeline's face value and not a promise (the "speed-to-lead" folklore stays in Chapter 4 where its sourcing is disclosed). Automation, when the volume justifies it: the touches above can fire automatically from a form or a missed call (Chapter 8's glue: a two-step automation on the free tiers covers "new row → reminder"; a text-back on a missed call pairs with Chapter 4's stack). One channel note before anything fires as a text: texting is its own legal lane (TCPA in the US, CASL in Canada), so any template that can go out as a text carries an opt-out line, and Chapter 4's law check runs before the switch flips. Automate the reminder and the draft first, keep the send manual until a month of reading drafts has taught you the failure shapes on your own leads.

After that watched month, automatic sending may begin only when the exact Appendix C card records PROMOTE TO CONTROLLED LIVE SEND for a frozen, human-approved lowest-stakes template with approved field substitution. That decision begins a separate controlled-live phase; it does not complete the hire. Confirm the failure with one week of missed-next-touch, duplicate, retrieval-time, or handoff counts before buying. In Canada, CASL can attach serious statutory penalties, and the sender carries the burden of proving the consent or other basis it relies on.
