Every dollar of cold machinery is better spent answering the phone (Chapter 4) and following the warm thread (this chapter). That's a take-back on an entire aisle of the store, and it stands until your business genuinely becomes an outbound B2B operation with a cleared process. The answer is judgment about your margin, your season, your read of the person — the half of the job Chapter 1 calls ceiling-work, and it doesn't delegate. Endless sequences and cold blasts. Chapter 7 A Lighter Back Office The back office is where your evenings go to die: the receipts in the console, the invoice you'll send "tonight," the meeting you'll definitely remember the details of (you won't), the books you'll catch up on Sunday. The measured claim, in your arithmetic: take your two audit numbers, halve them pessimistically, and price the checking ritual honestly into the tool's cost. The owner or qualified tax professional decides; filing software computes and populates forms only after verified answers. Reserve twenty minutes as the minimum, then clear every exception or add reviewer capacity; a growing queue does not become sampled away because the timer rang. Use the method local law requires. Park the tool until you've read its data page. No answer, hesitation, pressured staff agreement, or uncertainty means typed notes instead. Chapter 10 Probation: The Rollout You would never defend hiring a person, skipping the trial period, putting them on every job at once, and checking on them "eventually." A common failure pattern this book warns about — not a measured majority — is buying an AI tool in an optimistic hour, pointing it at everything, and reviewing it never. This chapter installs the missing employment practice: every tool starts on probation. One job, one metric measured against a baseline, firing criteria written before day one, and a weekly check-in that outlives the honeymoon. The standard unit is thirty days; customer-facing work and agents earn trust on stricter clocks below. The evidence for why comes from businesses much bigger than yours, and it should be read exactly at its labeled size.

Start at home: a Canadian survey of business leaders found 93% of organizations "using AI in some form" and only 2% seeing ROI (KPMG Canada, 2025; the sample skews large, so label it). MIT's much-quoted finding points the same way: 95% of formal enterprise AI pilots showed zero measurable return about six months on, under a narrow bar (deployed beyond pilot with measurable KPIs), an enterprise sample, and no small-business breakdown at all (MIT NANDA, 2025). S&P Global found AI-initiative abandonment at 42% of companies, with nearly half of proofs of concept scrapped before production (n=1,006, enterprise-wide, 2025). None of these is a statistic about your shop. The protected shorthand pilots fail where nobody owns the follow-through is this book's craft warning, not a finding from those studies; none proves why a pilot failed.

Bluevine's 2026 small-business survey (n=942, fielded July 2026; a small-business lender polling its own market, so label that too) found 78% of owners don't fully trust AI unsupervised. This chapter reads that distrust as the right instinct and builds it a schedule: supervision designed in, then trusted. After this chapter, you can: Sketch a probation card in five minutes, then prove its exit path before any data or live work enters Start and define a baseline in one week without new software; sparse workflows may need a month or longer Run the 30-minute weekly review that catches drift while it's cheap End each applicable probation phase with a written decision — never "we'll see" The primary build: the probation card and the weekly review The card (index card, note, whiteboard corner; one per exact tool, plan, account, and workflow, written BEFORE the trial starts).

Keep a tool registry listing every active workflow card. A new workflow, permission, data category, risk class, plan, or account starts its own card, gate, and clock; passing sanitized drafting never approves customer follow-up or live-data work: JOB: the one workflow this tool owns during probation. One. ("Answer after-hours calls and book them." Not "improve operations.") METRIC + BASELINE: the single number that says it's working, its denominator and eligibility rule, and a comparable prior period from your own records. Missed calls booked, quotes sent the same day, evening admin minutes. Predeclare the improvement large enough to matter and the minimum sample that could show it. If you can't name those, you're not ready to hire; run Chapter 7's audit first.

CHECKS: which named check from your failure map (Chapter 2's list of how machine work goes wrong, and the check for each) runs on its output, who runs it, and when. (A check that means listening to customer calls has a gate first: the tool announces recording in a way your state's or province's consent rule accepts.) During probation the cadence is doubled: what will be weekly forever is twice-weekly for 30 days. Sampling is the quality check, not the safety net: a job where a missed call is a gas smell or a burst pipe keeps a real-time human path (Chapter 4's urgent flag and emergency line) regardless of what the sample says.

KILL CRITERIA: written now, while you're sober: "Gone unless [rate or margin, with its denominator] beats a comparable baseline by [your meaningful number] after [minimum eligible observations], while staying below [maximum recoverable error or complaint rate], with zero red-line safety, privacy, legal, or irreversible incidents." One red-line incident permanently fires that exact card and workflow: contain it, switch to the tested fallback, close the incident, remedy affected people, and reconcile authoritative records. A materially redesigned successor is a new workflow and starts over with new qualified clearance, card, gates, and clock. Redesign-and-retry and the one extension apply only to recoverable defects or insufficient evidence.

If the minimum sample is too sparse by day 30, EXTEND ONCE is the inconclusive result; if the second window is still too sparse, FIRE — do not hire on hope. EXIT PATH: Probation you can't end isn't probation. Before data goes in, confirm the export and rehearse restore/import where the tool supports it and the state matters. Otherwise open, count, and sample the export, then rehearse a clean-account reconstruction from shop-held prompts, templates, facts, settings, and credential records. Also confirm the connected-system and credential inventory, one-action disable or rollback, manual fallback, authoritative-state reconciliation, retention/deletion handling, cancellation terms, and named owner sign-off. The five-minute card names this work; it does not prove it.
Here is one card filled in, a labeled illustration with round numbers, so yours has a model: JOB: answer after-hours calls (introducing itself as an assistant), book them into the calendar.

EXIT: spreadsheet export restore-tested; diversion to the staffed fallback tested; connections and credentials listed for removal; records reconciled from the last good run; deletion/retention and monthly cancellation confirmed; named owner signs off. Every field has a number, denominator, or name; that is the whole trick. Which clock applies? The card is universal. The clock is not. Use the riskiest row that touches the workflow; a hybrid inherits the stricter clock. Workflow class Before controlled live Controlled-live probation Final decision Reversible, non-destructive field transfer; no customer send, money, payroll, employment decision, access-control change, safety or regulated-status decision, or deletion

Workflow checks keep the weekly, real-time, or every-event cadence their own chapter requires): Metric vs. baseline (5 min). Read the number, write it on the card. Check the checks (10 min): confirm the named checks actually ran and re-read their notes (the honest question is "did I skip Thursday?"); no third sampling session — the week's two already happened. Contain it, switch to fallback, close the incident, remedy affected people, and reconcile authoritative records. A materially redesigned successor is new work with new clearance and a new clock. A recoverable defect that survived a check may use the single redesign extension with a fixed end date; a repeat past the redesigned check fires it.

For a bad price or promise already delivered, identify every affected customer, deliver the decided remedy, reconcile any money, and record evidence of closure the same day. An attempted callback is not closure. One decision (5 min): continue, adjust the script/instructions (Chapter 2, shape 5: corrections go in writing), or invoke the kill criteria early. Write it on the card. Every applicable phase ends with a written decision. For a narrow internal workflow, day 30 is Hire / Extend once / Fire. For a customer-send workflow, the watched month's first decision is Promote to controlled-live send / Extend once / Fire; promotion is not Hire, and a separate 30-day live phase follows. For an agent, day 30 is a midpoint, not a final decision; day 60 is Hire / Extend once / Fire.

Hire: the applicable final phase is complete, the metric cleared, and checks held; the tool joins the payroll, the card/metric review drops to monthly, every workflow-specific check keeps its chapter-defined cadence, and the card gets filed for Chapter 13's audits. Extend once: genuine externalities ate the phase or a recoverable redesign is underway; one extension, fixed new end date, same criteria, no paused fourth state; a second extension is a fire wearing a bathrobe. That line is your growing private database of what doesn't work in your shop, worth more than any review site. One workflow per card and per tool is the rule that makes all of it legible.

At most two disjoint workflows may be on probation concurrently, and only when they share no metric, data, system, or supervision bottleneck; three is how you end up unable to say which change moved the number. The measured claim, yours as always: a probation costs you the card sketch (five minutes to write, ten if you're deciding the numbers as you go), a separate pre-live block long enough to verify the exit and data gates, the baseline (usually free: last month's number off your own records, a week of counting only when no record exists), four-to-five weekly reviews (about two to two and a half hours total), and the doubled check cadence for the month: your named check, run twice a week instead of once, priced at whatever it costs you. That last line belongs on the tag.

Price all of it against the subscription's annual cost times the years it survives unused on autopay, and the ritual funds itself the first time it fires something. The take-backs, named The big-bang rollout. Everything-at-once adoption makes failures harder to attribute and unwind. Read Chapters 1–3 first, then choose one measured pain workflow from Chapters 4–9; their printed order is not a mandatory rollout sequence. A second disjoint workflow may run only under the two-card rule above. The unbaselined pilot. No before-number, no trial. A tool that can't be measured can't be fired, and unfireable workers run the shop (Chapter 1's owner-who-can't-fire line, now as procedure). "Set and forget." The drift Chapter 9 documented (supervision decaying as fit breeds trust) is the failure mode of successful pilots. The weekly-then-monthly review is not paranoia; it is the price on the tag.

A tool good enough to keep is important enough to check. Probation by demo. The trial runs on your real work, your real customers' shapes, with the fence intact: no customer data beyond what the live workflow itself requires enters the tool during probation (no bulk imports to see what it can do), and the export path is confirmed before any of it goes in (Chapter 12 carries the full fence). A tool that only shines on the vendor's sample data has passed the vendor's probation, not yours. Do this Friday About 25 minutes, $0 (step 5 is its own separate 20 minutes, and most readers need it). Pick the one workflow whose chapter you jumped to first when you read this book's map. That instinct was your prioritization; honor it. Sketch the probation card for the tool you're trialing or considering: five fields, pen, done. This is the five-minute artifact, not launch clearance.

Start the baseline if you don't have one: use the workflow-specific window and minimum sample you predeclared from event frequency, variability, seasonality, and the decision threshold. Rare safety, privacy, legal, or irreversible harms remain zero-tolerance regardless of sample. If the first clock cannot supply enough ordinary evidence, extend once; a second inconclusive window is FIRE or continue-manually, not permission to lower the bar. Calendar the pre-live verification block and the reviews for the applicable clock. The first block proves the exit path, data clearance, fallback, and rollback before launch; its duration depends on the connected tool and sits outside Friday's 25 minutes. A standard internal workflow gets four weekly reviews (add a fifth if day 30 lands past them); a customer-facing workflow gets reviews through both months; an agent gets reviews through day 60.

They are 30 minutes each, same slot. Treat them like payroll: they are. If a tool is already running un-probationed (most readers have one): budget a separate 20 minutes to write its card retroactively, baseline from old records, and give it a real day 30. Tenure requires a review it never had. The takeaway: every tool starts on probation — one job, one metric against a baseline, checks on a schedule, kill criteria written in advance, an exit confirmed before data goes in — and the workflow's own clock ends with a written decision, never drift.

Now the other direction, from bigger samples, with their own labels on: 82% of AI-adopting small businesses grew their workforce (US Chamber of Commerce, 2025), and 56% of small businesses say AI helps them offset headcount challenges (Verizon/Morning Consult, 2025). Both are industry surveys of self-reported experience, run by bodies with a stake in the sunny reading, and growing businesses adopt more of everything, so the arrow between AI and growth is not proven in either direction; read them as directional, the same grade as the worker-sentiment number below. The 56%, in this book's own reading of the survey-speak, mostly means we couldn't hire anyway, and the work still got done. That is the pattern this book has been documenting since Chapter 1: the pizza owner in Chapter 9 employs more people than before the AI took his phones.

At 1–10 staff, you don't usually employ a layer of identical tasks. You employ Maria, who does eleven things, four of which are floor-work. The machine may take those four; it cannot substitute cleanly for Maria's ceiling-work (the pricing call with a difficult regular) or her glue (she is the one who hears when a good customer sounds off). A five-person shop that cuts one person loses 20% of its hands while the machine may cover only the floor-work slice of what walked out. This book therefore chooses a capacity-first operating policy: use the machine to absorb floor-work, not as a pretext for a cut. That is a management commitment for this rollout, not a forecast or a promise that AI will never displace work or affect a role; the evidence above establishes no such immunity.

Which brings in the number that should shape how you speak: in a June 2026 online panel, 35.5% of 1,000 US working adults agreed or strongly agreed that working harder won't protect them from layoffs or AI (Founder Reports; cross-sectional self-report, not small-business staff specifically). Your team was not polled, but if the country's working adults are any guide, someone on your crew may already be quietly braced. Silence reads as confirmation. Map every role first (all of them, even at five minutes a role). Completing every role's fast screen and every required private one-to-one is a blocking prerequisite to any group talk. Only then say the true thing, once, plainly, and early. One version, in this book's words (yours will be better): "I'm using AI for repetitive work — drafts, retyping, scheduling.

This rollout is designed to increase capacity, and no reduction is currently planned because of it. Your jobs will tilt toward the parts that need a person, and checking the machine's work is going to be part of how we all work now. If plans change, you'll hear it from me first, directly and lawfully, not from a tool announcement." Say it your way and keep it to present intent and the truth you can support; future business conditions are not yours to guarantee. Have a local employment adviser review any job-security assurance before you give it. Being caught managing your people by stealth costs more than any of Chapter 12's legal trouble, but so does a promise you had no authority to make. The solo professional's version, faced

Friday's slot picks the engagements and ropes off the time; the real math is its own sitting this week, an hour or more with last year's numbers. You don't have to send the new prices yet. Chapter 12 Stay Out of Trouble: Data, Promises, and Compliance When you hire a person, a century of employment law tells you what you owe each other. When you hire the machine, one Canadian tribunal held Air Canada responsible on one set of facts. That is not a universal liability rule; it is enough reason for a conservative operating rule: be prepared to answer for what your tools say. Jake Moffatt booked an Air Canada flight after the airline's website chatbot explained a bereavement-fare policy: book now, claim the discount within 90 days. That version of the policy didn't exist. Air Canada's real bereavement policy required asking before the flight; the book-now-claim-later part was the bot's invention. The airline refused to honor it, and argued, in effect, that the chatbot was responsible for its own words.

The British Columbia Civil Resolution Tribunal disagreed and made Air Canada pay: CA$812.02, the fare difference plus interest and fees (Moffatt v. Air Canada, February 2024). Note the venue honestly: a provincial small-claims-style tribunal, eight hundred dollars, no grand precedent machinery. The ruling binds nobody else, and whether any bot statement is legally binding depends on the facts and local law. The risk-management lesson is still useful: treat every bot statement as something your business may have to answer for. This book turns that into house policy, not a universal legal theorem: Every promise your tools make becomes your incident to own and resolve. Nothing unsafe, unlawful, impossible, or above the approved make-good limit gets performed without the Rule 3 escalation.

Chapter 4 warned you when you switched the phones on; this chapter turns the warning into your shop's one-page policy. One scope line before the rules: this chapter does not cover AI used to make or recommend employment decisions (hiring, firing, scheduling, pay, promotion, discipline, accommodation, or anything like them). That class needs its own employment-law and human-rights review, with qualified counsel, before any use; nothing on this page clears it. The other legal fact of machine labor you already know from Chapter 2: the machine gives confidently wrong answers about rules. New York City's own official business-help chatbot told owners to break laws it existed to explain. So the two exposure paths are now mapped: what the machine promises outward (your liability to customers) and what the machine tells you inward (compliance advice that's wrong).

One policy page covers both, plus the quiet third exposure most owners never price: what you feed in. Consumer and business plans can differ by provider, account, region, age, contract, and product surface. Defaults, menu paths, retention periods, and data-use terms move. Before real work, open the current first-party documentation for the exact plan and account, record the date and policy version or save a snapshot, and read back which subprocessors are used and what training, retention, sharing, and deletion controls actually apply. If that direct record is missing or unclear, no live data enters the tool. A disabled training control is necessary where available, never sufficient: it does not erase retention, provider access, subprocessors, safety review, legal demands, or breach risk. Live data still needs the clearance below. After this chapter, you can:

Yours is one page on the wall, three rules, dated and signed by everyone who touches a work account, you first, and by every new hire before their first login to a work account: day one, not quarter-end. The three rules answer the three exposures in the order you can control them: what goes in, what goes out, what you believe. Copy the box below as the wall policy.

The longer rules after it are implementation notes, not extra wall copy. No chatbot settles a legal, tax, safety, employment, privacy, accounting, insurance, or compliance question. Use the controlling primary source and the qualified professional for the decision. Until the affected workflow is re-cleared, freeze new affected live-data intake and use the tested manual fallback. Implementation notes for the three rules RULE 1 — WHAT GOES IN.

Nothing we'd have to apologize for losing. Consumer assistants receive only synthetic, sanitized, or non-personal material. An approved business processor receives only the minimum necessary fields after the exact-workflow clearance below. Credentials, passwords, API keys, authentication codes, recovery secrets, payment or banking secrets, and security configurations never enter any assistant. Identity documents, children's data, health data, employee records, tax, legal, accounting, insurance, or disciplinary files, trade secrets, source code, unpublished financials, material under an NDA, and other specially regulated or contract-bound material remain out unless a qualified review establishes a separate controlled process. This list is not exhaustive; uncertainty means stop. Work uses shop-controlled accounts whose current terms and settings have been recorded.

Meetings require an affirmative yes from every participant before recording or transcription. Phone-line recording stays off until the exact disclosure/consent flow is documented against official guidance or cleared by a qualified local privacy/compliance professional; stricter contractual, professional, workplace, provincial, or state rules still govern. Any tool that stores recordings gets its exact plan's data page read before the first meeting: storage, sharing, retention, deletion, and training use. The test for gray areas: would you pin it to the shop door? Then it doesn't go in the chat either. LIVE-DATA CLEARANCE — required before any connection. The one-page policy does not itself clear live people or business data.

For each exact tool, plan, account, and workflow, complete Appendix B and record evidence, date, and named owner for: operating and data-subject jurisdictions; applicable federal, provincial/state, sector, workplace, health, and contractual rules; minimum necessary fields; purpose and lawful authority or consent; privacy-impact-assessment threshold and result; privacy-officer or qualified-review sign-off where required; vendor/processor agreement; subprocessors; storage and cross-border transfer; data-subject rights; access and security; training/data-use settings; retention and deletion; required notices; breach terms and incident process; export; and the workflow's pre-live test, fallback, and rollback. Sensitive, regulated, contract-bound, cross-border, or uncertain processing gets qualified local privacy/security advice before connection.

Any blank, uncertain, or failed field means NO LIVE CONNECTION. A row may be N/A only when the worksheet records the legal or contractual basis for that conclusion, its evidence, date, and owner; N/A is not a substitute for uncertainty. RULE 2 — WHAT GOES OUT. Three classes, no ambiguity. (1) New or changed generated customer language remains a draft until a person reads and approves it; it never earns autonomous promotion. (2) Fixed, human-approved templates may send automatically only after the Chapter 6 and Chapter 8 gates and the exact Appendix C card pass; approved field substitution is allowed, generated or paraphrased wording is not. (3) A receptionist may play only exact, deterministic, pre-approved templates and fill pre-approved slots after Chapter 4's phone gates and Appendix C pass, including a technically supported shadow mode.

If the tool cannot support one, customer-facing promotion is prohibited. Free-form interpretation may only classify intent and select a frozen approved response or slot after the same canonical gate; it may not generate customer-facing wording. Appendix C is the single authority for event floors, watched periods, controlled-live clocks, promotion, and final decisions; this page adds no shorter route. Any paraphrase or other new language stays a draft or hands to a person; everything outside the templates and slots hands off. Every introduced or changed number, date, price, deadline, guarantee, or commitment is source-checked against the controlling record and recalculated where arithmetic applies. No improvised policies, prices, or guarantees, because of the airline story on the back of this page.

If a tool makes a promise anyway, treat it as an incident: in Moffatt, the misstatement produced a CA$812.02 total award, including damages, interest, and tribunal fees. The page names the largest make-good we'd honor without a meeting, and that number is internal goodwill and escalation guidance only: never a legal limit, and never a basis to deny what the business actually owes. Anything above it, and any promise touching regulated, safety, financial, contract, or reliance-sensitive ground, escalates under Rule 3 to a person with the appropriate counsel or adviser in the loop, fast and honest, before anything is acted on. Escalation is a decision point, not an automatic no: the reviewer decides how to honor, correct, negotiate, or resolve it.

The same day, name the incident owner and deadline, identify and contact every affected customer, deliver the decided remedy, reconcile any money, record evidence of closure, and fix the script. A vendor fix never closes a customer's incident; the error survived its check, so the task comes back (Chapter 1's firing rule, now company policy). RULE 3 — WHAT WE BELIEVE. Rules come from the source of the rule. No legal, tax, safety, or compliance question gets settled by a chatbot, ours or anyone's; the NYC story is what official-looking wrongness looks like. The machine may brief the professional (draft our questions, organize our documents); the professional or the primary source decides.

And no AI checks another AI's work and calls it verified: a Texas lawyer tried exactly that, the second tool missed the fabrications, and the court ordered a $2,000 payment to its registry plus mandatory AI education (Chapter 2 carries the case and its record). Checks run against reality: our documents, our numbers, the actual regulation, a qualified human. Those are the implementation notes. The printable box already carries the disclosure, handoff, and review footers; the details here explain how to operate them. This book's conservative house policy says the bot identifies itself as AI up front and offers the staffed human path during documented coverage hours; outside those hours it uses the fixed no-human script and backup path from Chapter 4.

Recording, telemarketing, consumer-protection, accessibility, and sector-specific notices remain separate jurisdiction-specific gates; the wall sentence does not pretend they are one universal bot-disclosure law. Re-read the page at the quarterly audit (Chapter 13) and re-check the recorded plan terms and controls with it, because tools and menus change, and a policy that nobody re-reads is a poster, not a policy. The measured claim, computable as always, and recomputed the way Rule 2 demands: ten minutes of switches, 40 minutes of writing, and five for the bot check — about 55 minutes for Friday's first policy draft. The separate team talk happens on paid time and is part of the price too; budget fifteen minutes for a small crew, then record what it actually takes. That under-two-hour block buys the policy shell, not permission to connect live data.

Each exact workflow's Appendix B clearance, vendor-document hunt, account migration, any qualified privacy/security advice, incident investigation, staff training beyond the talk, weekly sampling, and quarterly review are separate recurring or one-time lines to price before launch. Compare the whole cost with one Moffatt-sized make-good (CA$812, in the real case), one lost client whose data you'd have to confess to pasting, or one afternoon untangling advice a bot invented. And those are the cheap failures: a leaked health or payment record can carry breach-notification duties and statutory exposure, a number with more digits than any make-good. The take-backs, named "The AI said it was legal." Do not treat that as a defense you can count on.

This book's policy recognizes none, and the machine offers no professional standard or remedy behind the answer; Rule 3 exists so the sentence is never uttered in your shop. Compliance-by-chatbot. Minimum wage, tips, scheduling laws, tax thresholds: source-of-rule or professional, every time. Free answers about laws are priced exactly right. The unattended bot with a wide script. Every capability you add to a customer-facing bot is surface area on Rule 2. Keep the script narrow, keep a person ready to step in, and sample its answers weekly (Chapter 9's ritual). A bot you can't audit this week is a bot you shouldn't run this week. Personal accounts for work. The cheapest data leak there is: work pasted into an account whose settings, retention, and training status you've never seen.

Work uses a shop-controlled account; set available opt-outs, then complete Appendix B before any live data or connection. An opt-out is one control, never clearance. The oldest-chats sweep and the paid team talk are separate scheduled work; migration, investigation, further training, weekly sampling, and the quarterly review also keep their own time. Tonight, the controls (10 min for the accounts you hold): open the current first-party record for each exact account, record the plan, region, date, and policy version or saved snapshot, and read back the applicable data-use, retention, sharing, and deletion controls. Screenshot settings pages, not chat contents; those screenshots and policy records are your diligence appendix.

Staff on personal accounts is its own job: this week, ask what each person actually uses and move the work onto shop-controlled accounts, priced in days, not in tonight's ten minutes. Then scroll your oldest chats once (call it 15 minutes, its own box, outside the 60-minute policy draft): whatever got pasted last year may still be sitting there. If you find sensitive content, stop. Freeze further business use and affected integrations; secure the account; revoke shared sessions, links, or tokens as appropriate; name an incident lead the same day; assess connected systems and prior exposure; rotate credentials when compromise is plausible; and invoke the tested manual fallback. Do not copy, export, or screenshot the payload casually. Record only necessary metadata — account, date, data category, people affected if known, access, and actions — in the secured incident log.

Preserve content only under the incident lead's or adviser's direction, in controlled storage. If your organization is subject to PIPEDA, keep the required breach record for 24 months; separately assess whether reporting and notification are required under the real-risk threshold and applicable law. Delete only what the incident plan or adviser clears. A customer's card number or health detail is a Rule 3 call now: get qualified privacy help this week, not at the quarterly. The retention period never delays containment or the call. Write the page and install the clearance form (40 min): adapt the three rules above in your own words and examples, then copy Appendix B beside it as the required per-tool live-data clearance record. Every row gets evidence, date, owner, and a pass/no-live decision. Keep the policy itself to one page even if it hurts; the clearance records sit behind it.

The talk (budget 15 min, schedule it today): walk the page, everyone signs, it goes on the wall and in the drive. Six staff at the counter often finishes in five, not a conference; solo means you sign it and mean it; a dispersed or shift crew means catching each person once this week, a few minutes each, with the time scaling by headcount, not by this page. Pair it with Chapter 11's speech only after every Chapter 11 role screen, required private one-to-one, and applicable employment-adviser review is complete. Otherwise this meeting covers only data-use policy; schedule the headcount talk separately. The bot audit (5 min, if you run one): read your customer-facing bot's script against Rule 2. If it could make a promise you would not honor, divert it to the tested manual fallback now.

Edit a non-live copy, rerun the affected Appendix C tests, and resume only after the card owner records the pass. If a defect may already have reached customers, reconcile the bot log against calls, bookings, complaints, refunds, transfers, and payments; name the owner and deadline, contact affected customers, deliver and reconcile the remedy, and close the incident with evidence. The takeaway: your business owns what its machines leak, say, and believe — so run one page and three rules: nothing confidential goes in; no new or generated customer wording goes out unread (a frozen approved template still needs the full lifecycle); and rules come from the source of the rule, never the bot.

You don't need any of those numbers to be precise. You need one statement sweep to learn your own. Every AI, automation, newly added, materially changed, or materially risky workflow has its own current probation card (Chapter 10), each metric still clears, and each check still runs. A generic tool-level card is not enough for those workflows. Established non-AI infrastructure instead needs one current critical-system record per tool/account: owner, active users, dependencies, authoritative data, access controls, current cost and renewal, backup/restore or reconstruction evidence, continuity path, incident route, and last review. That record is sufficient under this book unless a new AI/automation use, live-data purpose, material change, or material risk triggers Appendix B and probation. It enters PROVE only when the record is missing, a trigger appears, or evidence fails; do not freeze ordinary service merely because long-used non-AI infrastructure lacks an AI-workflow card.

At the first audit, an uncarded triggered workflow is PROVE. Preserve service through the tested manual or human fallback; unproven customer-facing AI returns to watched draft or shadow mode. Historical records can preserve a phase only when they fill every field and prove that exact current workflow cleared it. If Appendix B clearance is missing for the triggered workflow, stop new intake and, where safe, pause its ongoing processing, disclosure, scheduled jobs, and affected integrations; preserve evidence and use the tested fallback. Open the Chapter 12 assessment for potentially affected data and connected systems, contain plausible ongoing exposure, then narrow the response to what the evidence shows was processed; do not freeze unaffected established non-AI service. Billing hygiene lives here too: downgrade annual-renewing Keeps you over-bought.

Follow Chapter 3's first-year month-to-month rule; after that, compare the annual saving in writing against lock-in and exit risk before prepaying. PROVE. You feel it's useful but there's no card and no number, or it is a tool whose metric no longer clears. It gets a card today (or an updated one) and the applicable Chapter 10 re-probation with real kill criteria. Feelings don't make payroll; numbers do. A tool you can't name the job of in one sentence starts here at best, and falls straight through to Exit if it also fails the number and opened-it-lately tests. Worked once (say, the transcription tool a busy March added): the feeling is real, the card isn't. Card today, every review date for the correct clock on the calendar. EXIT. No job, no number, no opened-it-lately. Cancellation is the verdict you cannot undo, so the exit gate is objective.

Identify statutory and contractual retention duties; export the authoritative records plus attachments and history; open, count, and sample them; reconcile the final authoritative state; identify the owner, active users, connected systems, recent API or activity logs, and downstream jobs; prove the manual continuity path; and read the renewal terms. Annual contracts may require advance written notice through a specified channel, and an in-app cancel may not count; read the exact renewal and cancellation clause. A cheap connector may never be opened and still move booking data every night, so an uncleared dependency stays in Prove. If the tool held client data, Chapter 12's fence applies on the way out: confirm deletion, backups, legal holds, and subprocessors, not just the export. A named owner signs off on retention, completeness, operational cutoff, and fallback before cancellation.

Once those checks clear: Cancel today, not "after I check whether we use it" — the audit was the check. Follow contract terms, provide required notice, complete the in-app flow where applicable, and calendar the effective deadline. Expect the vendor to fight the leaving harder than it sold the joining: the discount offer, the guilt screen. Worked once, on the book's own confession: the author's $5 voice tool from Chapter 1 sorts in one breath. Job it was hired for? A voice studio nobody has opened in half a year. Number? None. An Exit by the audit's own rules, and if the author hesitates over five dollars, the hesitation is data there too. And one more column, for any tool that touches customer or client data, whatever its verdict: has its data page changed since you last read it? Retention, training, sharing.

On the first audit, save a dated PDF or snapshot, or record the vendor's policy-version identifier, plus the key terms: training, sharing, subprocessors, country, retention, deletion, and breach handling. Every later audit compares against that preserved record, not a mutable URL and a date. A changed answer moves even a Keep to Prove, because the tool you audited is not the tool it just became. If the change adds a new use of customer data, immediately freeze new affected live-data intake and integrations, invoke the tested manual fallback, map the affected data and jurisdictions, and compare the change with your privacy notice and preserved record. Get the required qualified local privacy/security review and re-run Chapter 12 and Appendix B before resuming.

If the change already took effect, assess already-processed data under the incident procedure; later review cannot undo an affected disclosure or retention. Chapter 12's page is where both live. Step 3, the policy re-read (10 min). The one-page AI policy from Chapter 12 (what goes in; why no new or generated customer wording goes out unread while frozen approved templates still need the full lifecycle; where rules come from), out loud if there's a team. Tools changed this quarter; the page has to have met them. Step 4, the learning budget (20 min now, capped at two hours a quarter total). Here is the calm-owner claim, stated plainly: a quarterly cadence is enough, on purpose. The AI market's churn is spectacular: the directory that counts such things lists some 47,400 AI tools — its own counter, and bigness is its business.

A tracker of dead AI products has logged 106 casualties as of August 2026 (a directional tally), and no trusted, shop-scale Consumer Reports-style authority exists in the retained record. Those facts point the same way: the noise is the vendors' race, not your homework. Neither names the right interval, though: quarterly is this book's call, sized to a calendar you'll actually keep, not a finding from any study. Your two hours: your trade association's take on anything new in your vertical, one practitioner source you trust in your actual trade, and a skim of your kept tools' changelogs for price or data-policy changes (which feed the audit above). That's it. The FOMO engine (every "the businesses that adopt X this quarter will bury the ones that don't" ad) is Chapter 3's who-profits question answering itself: anxiety is the product, and the subscription is the treatment being sold.

You are not behind. You are audited, which is different, and rarer. It is the thing this book has been building since the first evening: an owner whose tools have jobs, checks, cards, and firing dates is done keeping up, because there is nothing to keep up with except her own numbers. The measured claim, in your handwriting as always: first-year net audit benefit = avoidable subscription cost actually eliminated during the next twelve months − triage labor − remediation and exit labor − professional fees − cancellation or overlap costs. Show the ongoing annual run-rate saving separately. De la Garza's two hours found four figures, by her own account; yours might find a tenth of that, and the arithmetic still works only after your full costs are included.

The book promises no number, and after thirteen chapters you know that's not modesty: numbers you didn't compute yourself don't get believed here, and that includes the book's, and hers. One last Exit gate before the take-backs: open the export, compare counts, and sample records and their attachments, notes, and history. Test restore/import where the tool supports it and the state matters; otherwise rehearse a clean-account reconstruction from shop-held prompts, templates, facts, settings, and credential records. Store a protected backup and have the named owner sign off.

Reserve a separate follow-up block for each Chapter 10 probation card and day-30 review; the five card fields and their exit/data proof do not fit inside Friday's first hour. Calendar next quarter's triage (two hours, thirteen weeks out), the separate two-hour learning budget, and every remediation block your hours-and-fees columns exposed. Then close the laptop only after each open repair has an owner and date. The cadence is enough to find the work; the repair time is measured separately. The takeaway: your tools are a payroll — audit it quarterly into Keep, Prove, or Exit with yearly numbers, cap the keeping-up at two hours a quarter, and let the market churn without you; calm is what an audited stack feels like.

Machine labor comes in three rungs of independence, and the book has been walking you up them in order. Rung one: the assistant. Work happens when you ask, one task at a time, checked as it lands. The drafting, summarizing, and analysis work in Chapters 4 through 7 lives here. In this book's judgment, most businesses should spend most of their first year on rung one, and a year there is not slow; it is how the checking habits form while the stakes are small. Rung two: automations. Work happens on triggers without your hands (Chapter 8's couriers), but each deterministic trigger, transfer, and fixed-template step follows a recipe you wrote. The failure shape is repetition and the check is the run log.

Appendix C is the single authority for its adversarial tests, shadow evidence, customer-facing watched period, controlled-live probation, and final decision; generated or paraphrased customer language never earns autonomous promotion. A hybrid workflow is graded by its riskiest component, inheriting rung one's invention and misreading checks as well as rung two's run controls. A transfer bot and an open-ended AI receptionist are not the same hire. Rung three: agents. Software that plans multi-step work on its own: reads the inbox, decides what matters, acts, remembers. This rung is real, and this book's honest report is that at owner scale it is early. One secondhand account at anything like your size describes Scott Bell, a solo bankruptcy lawyer, running a small fleet of open-source agents on OpenClaw.

The reported arc reads like a trust ladder: months of specifying "every teensy step," an orchestrator taking notes, and only then delegated judgment such as flagging court notices and drafting reply ideas. Nobody interviewed his clients, audited an agent's decision, or resolved the professional-supervision question. It is unverified context, not evidence that the approach is safe or effective. The same platform's public record that season includes reported inbox deletion despite stop commands and fabricated board figures (TechCrunch, Feb 2026; Business Insider, Mar 2026). The rung-three verdict by the book's own instrument: agents concentrate exactly what Chapter 1 taught you to price. Wide blast radius, expensive verification. So they inherit the strictest version of every rule, not a waiver.

If you climb in year one: one agent, one read-only job on copies; least-privilege credentials; no send, delete, edit, or other outside effect without approval for that action; a tested stop control; a verified backup and rollback; no money movement or unsupervised customer contact; probation doubled from Chapter 10's standard 30 days to 60; run logs read weekly. An agent may prepare a purchase packet or cart only. A human independently opens the first-party payment interface, verifies vendor, amount, destination, and terms, and executes the purchase; no standing approval exists. Human approval tests only that exact non-purchase action, not a wider privilege, and any new action or permission restarts the gate and 60-day clock. If the tool cannot meet that fence, wait.

Rungs one and two carry every checkable win this book teaches, your own probation cards will tell you what they returned, and rung three will still be there once it has a track record. One contrast case, for calibrated ambition rather than fever: Base44, launched by a single founder in January 2025, was acquired by Wix that June, five months in, for a reported $80 million upfront (TechCrunch, Jun 2025). The revenue and profit figures along the way were the founder's own, unaudited. The sources document nothing about his verification process, so no moral about "judgment" gets to ride on it. It happened; it is not a plan. The plan is the boring ladder, climbed at the speed of your checks. Signals a tool is dying, and the switch/sit rule Tools die; a tracker exists just to log AI products that didn't make it. You don't need to predict failures, only to notice the four signals early:

The changelog goes quiet: no updates in two quarters while the category moves. Price hikes arrive with nothing attached: monetizing the trapped. Support you once had degrades to a bot with no human path: a vendor that removes its human lane has stopped investing in keeping you. (A tool that was always bot-first gets judged on the other three.) The data-export door narrows: exit risk has increased, whatever the vendor's reason. One hard signal — an export restriction, shutdown notice, security or privacy deterioration, or loss of critical support — triggers the contingency plan. For security or privacy deterioration, freeze new live-data intake and affected integrations immediately, invoke the tested manual fallback, name the incident owner, assess prior exposure, and require full Chapter 12 re-clearance before resuming. Export safely under the incident plan rather than widening exposure.

For the other hard signals, run the tested export while it still works. Any two softer signals together (a starting rule, not a statute) move the tool to Prove at the next audit. If the tool held customer data, ask the vendor to confirm in writing what was deleted, when, which backups or legal holds remain, what subprocessors retain, and whether any past model training can be reversed. And the switch/sit rule for the shinier direction, new tools: switch on your numbers, sit on the market's. Your probation card's metric sagging, your checks catching more, your audit finding a better-fitting Keep: switch. A launch video, a competitor's ad, a headline about the model that changes everything: sit. Chapter 13 already capped your exposure to the second kind at two hours a quarter; this rule is what those hours are for.
